cards.title: Which huge-object properties need only a few bit queries per sample?
cards.formal: Characterize the label-invariant distribution properties whose DoHO query complexity is at most poly(1/ε)·Õ(s(n,ε/2)), where s is the sample complexity of testing the same property in the DoHO model. Both complexities use earth-mover distance induced by normalized Hamming distance on n-bit strings. The source gives positive and negative examples, so the target is a classification rather than a universal bound for every property.
cards.why: Would identify when testing a distribution of enormous objects can exploit sampling without paying to read each object, clarifying the relationship between statistical information and local access cost.
cards.status_note: Read the primary model and full question, the corrected May 2023 version including its explicit erratum, and the 2025 uniformity/grainedness results. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no general classification. The form of the requested characterization still needs specification.

sentences: The DoHO model samples long bit strings but charges the tester for every inspected bit.
Distance between distributions is earth-mover distance using normalized Hamming costs.
The source asks which label-invariant properties need only polynomial-in-accuracy and logarithmic overhead over their DoHO sample complexity.
Its corrected full version weakens one claimed general transfer theorem, while a 2025 paper sharpens bounds for a particular uniformity property.
A precise general characterization criterion remains to be specified.

cards.definitions: For each n≥1, a property Dₙ is a set of probability distributions on Ωₙ={0,1}ⁿ. It is label-invariant if P∈Dₙ exactly when π_*P∈Dₙ for every bijection π:Ωₙ→Ωₙ, where (π_*P)(y)=P(π^{-1}(y)). This permits arbitrary permutations of all strings, not merely permutations of bit coordinates. For x,y∈Ωₙ let h(x,y)=n^{−1}|{j:xⱼ≠yⱼ}|. Define W_H(P,Q)=min_w Σ_{x,y}w(x,y)h(x,y), where w≥0 has row sums P and column sums Q. The distance to Dₙ is inf_{Q∈Dₙ}W_H(P,Q). A DoHO tester is a randomized algorithm given n and rational ε∈(0,1), with access to independent samples X¹,X²,…∼P. A sample is an oracle for an n-bit string: querying a pair (i,j) reveals only Xⁱⱼ, and further queries to that sample reveal bits of the same string. The algorithm may adapt which sample and coordinate to query. It must accept P∈Dₙ with probability at least 2/3 and reject when inf_{Q∈Dₙ}W_H(P,Q)>ε with probability at least 2/3, with no requirement in the intermediate region. Probability includes samples and internal randomness. Sample complexity counts the maximum number of independent sample oracles required; query complexity counts the maximum total number of inspected bits. The reference sample complexity permits arbitrarily many bit queries to those samples. The comparison seeks only polynomial losses in 1/ε and logarithmic factors in the sample bound, not a factor n for reading every sampled object. It does not compare against total-variation testing in the standard model, where each sample is revealed in full and closeness has a different definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify and prove a non-tautological necessary-and-sufficient characterization for the label-invariant property families satisfying the stated query-versus-DoHO-sample comparison, with explicit uniformity and polynomial/logarithmic losses. The source does not yet specify the form of this characterization. A sufficient condition alone, a result comparing to standard-model sample complexity, or bounds for a single property do not complete the general classification.

context_blocks.title: A sample can be much larger than the tester can read
context_blocks.text: The input distribution generates n-bit objects. Access to one sampled object does not reveal its entire label for free; the tester pays separately for each inspected bit.

context_blocks.title: Distance accounts for the geometry of the objects
context_blocks.text: Moving probability mass between similar strings costs their relative Hamming distance. This earth-mover metric can be much smaller than total variation, even for a label-invariant property.

context_blocks.title: The conference version overclaimed one general transfer
context_blocks.text: The corrected full version explicitly retracts its earlier use of DoHO sample complexity in the theorem for properties closed under arbitrary mappings. The corrected theorem starts from standard-model sample complexity, a weaker comparison. It leaves the stronger DoHO-sample version open.

context_blocks.title: There are both positive and negative cases
context_blocks.text: Bounded-support testing gives a positive example. For uniformity over a prescribed number m of strings, bit-query complexity can be nearly linear in m even though only about m^{2/3} full samples are needed at constant accuracy. Thus label invariance by itself is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: The 2025 refinement remains a special-property result
context_blocks.text: For parameterized uniformity and m≤n, the new theorem gives an Ω(m/log m) query lower bound and matches known upper bounds up to logarithms. For other ranges it supplies an O(m^{2/3}n) query algorithm, emphasizing that the parameters matter.

context_blocks.title: Remaining formulation issue
context_blocks.text: The source asks for a characterization of the properties satisfying the comparison, rather than asserting that every label-invariant property does. It does not specify an admissible form or effective representation for the desired characterization. A precise single benchmark needs that criterion and its uniformity conventions; listing more examples or restating the inequality as the definition of the class is not a characterization of the intended kind.

cards.context:
The input distribution generates n-bit objects. Access to one sampled object does not reveal its entire label for free; the tester pays separately for each inspected bit.

Moving probability mass between similar strings costs their relative Hamming distance. This earth-mover metric can be much smaller than total variation, even for a label-invariant property.

The corrected full version explicitly retracts its earlier use of DoHO sample complexity in the theorem for properties closed under arbitrary mappings. The corrected theorem starts from standard-model sample complexity, a weaker comparison. It leaves the stronger DoHO-sample version open.

Bounded-support testing gives a positive example. For uniformity over a prescribed number m of strings, bit-query complexity can be nearly linear in m even though only about m^{2/3} full samples are needed at constant accuracy. Thus label invariance by itself is insufficient.

For parameterized uniformity and m≤n, the new theorem gives an Ω(m/log m) query lower bound and matches known upper bounds up to logarithms. For other ranges it supplies an O(m^{2/3}n) query algorithm, emphasizing that the parameters matter.

The source asks for a characterization of the properties satisfying the comparison, rather than asserting that every label-invariant property does. It does not specify an admissible form or effective representation for the desired characterization. A precise single benchmark needs that criterion and its uniformity conventions; listing more examples or restating the inequality as the definition of the class is not a characterization of the intended kind.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
